See how you translated the expression “burden” in [13:1](ta:13). Alternate translation: [A message about]

Here Isaiah is speaking of Jerusalem as if it were **the Valley of Vision**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Jerusalem, the city of vision]

1.q: מַה לָּ֣⁠ךְ אֵפ֔וֹא כִּֽי עָלִ֥ית כֻּלָּ֖⁠ךְ לַ⁠גַּגּֽוֹת
1.note: Isaiah is using the question form to express rebuke and amazement at the people’s behavior. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [How wrong it is, then, that you have gone up, all of you, to the housetops!]

The word **you** is feminine singular in this verse, and the words “you” and “your” are feminine singular in verses 2, 3, and 7, because they refer to the city of Jerusalem, which is being personified as a woman. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction, and use the feminine form if your language marks that distinction.

Isaiah is using **What to you** as a common expression of his culture to ask the people why they have gone to their rooftops. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [What is the matter with you, then]

2.q: תְּשֻׁא֣וֹת מְלֵאָ֗ה עִ֚יר הֽוֹמִיָּ֔ה קִרְיָ֖ה עַלִּיזָ֑ה
2.note: Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [The clamoring city is full of noises; the exultant town is full of noise]

The expressions **the clamoring city** and **the exultant town** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two expressions together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the noisy, celebrating city]

Here, **the sword** represents a fight between soldiers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [soldiers killed while fighting the enemy]

3.note: Isaiah says **All of your leaders have fled together** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [Every last one of your leaders has fled together]

The expression **they have been bound** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the enemy bound them]

Isaiah is using **without a bow** as a common expression of the culture to mean “without putting up a fight.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [without putting up a fight] or [without defending themselves]

Isaiah says **All of your found ones have been bound together** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [Not one of your found ones escaped being bound together]

The expression **have been bound together** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the enemy bound together]
The pronoun **they** refers to the ones who were found. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [those who were found had fled far away]

4.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please look away from me]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please let me weep bitterly]

The word **you** and the implied “you” in the imperative **Look away** are plural because Isaiah is addressing the people of the city of Jerusalem. The word “you” is plural for the same reason in verses 9–11 and 14. So in all of these instances, use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction, and use the masculine form if your language marks that distinction.

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please do not try to comfort me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how they destroyed]

Here Isaiah is speaking of the people of Jerusalem as if they were a **daughter**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my people in Jerusalem]

5.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **tumult** and **trampling** and **confusion**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [people shouting, being trampled, and running in all directions]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **breaking down**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [walls breaking down]

6.note: Isaiah is using the word translated as **And** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

Isaiah is speaking of the nation of **Elam** as if it were an individual person, its ancestor, whose name was Elam. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The warriors of Elam carried their quivers]

Isaiah is speaking of the nation of **Kir** as if it were an individual person, its ancestor, whose name was Kir. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the soldiers of Kir uncovered their shields]

7.note: Isaiah is using the phrase translated as **And it happened** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

The expression **your valleys became full of chariotry** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [chariotry filled your valleys]

Isaiah is repeating forms of the verb **set** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [stationed themselves firmly]

8.note: Here Isaiah is speaking of Judah’s defenses as if they were a **covering**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the enemy removed Judah’s defensive covering]

The verb that the ULT translates as **you looked** could be third-person feminine singular or second-person masculine singular. Those two forms coincide in the case of this verb. If it is feminine singular, then it is a personification of the city of Jerusalem as a woman, as in verses 1–3 and 7. If it is the masculine singular form of “you,” it would be addressing a representative Israelite. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. If you do, use the singular form of “you” in your translation if your language marks that distinction, and use the feminine form if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [and he looked] or [and one looked]

The expression **the House of the Forest** refers to a specific building in Jerusalem that Solomon had built to store weapons. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could make this implicit information explicit. Alternate translation: [the House of the Forest, which was Solomon’s armory]

10.q: וְ⁠אֶת בָּתֵּ֥י יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם סְפַרְתֶּ֑ם וַ⁠תִּתְֿצוּ֙ הַ⁠בָּ֣תִּ֔ים לְ⁠בַצֵּ֖ר הַ⁠חוֹמָֽה
10.note: The word translated as **to** indicates the purpose for counting and tearing down **the houses of Jerusalem**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is the purpose for the action that came before. Alternate translation: [in order to strengthen the city wall]

11.q: וּ⁠מִקְוָ֣ה עֲשִׂיתֶ֗ם בֵּ֚ין הַ⁠חֹ֣מֹתַ֔יִם לְ⁠מֵ֖י הַ⁠בְּרֵכָ֣ה הַ⁠יְשָׁנָ֑ה וְ⁠לֹ֤א הִבַּטְתֶּם֙ אֶל עֹשֶׂ֔י⁠הָ וְ⁠יֹצְרָ֥⁠הּ מֵֽ⁠רָח֖וֹק לֹ֥א רְאִיתֶֽם
11.note: The word translated as **But** indicates a contrast between what came before and what follows. Use a connector in your language that makes this contrast clear. Alternate translation: [And you made a reservoir between the two walls for the waters of the old pool. Yet you did not look to its maker, and you did not regard the one having formed it long ago]

11.q: וְ⁠לֹ֤א הִבַּטְתֶּם֙ אֶל־ עֹשֶׂ֔י⁠הָ וְ⁠יֹצְרָ֥⁠הּ מֵֽ⁠רָח֖וֹק לֹ֥א רְאִיתֶֽם
11.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [But you did not look to its maker; no, you did not regard the one having formed it long ago]
The pronoun **its** refers to the pool of water. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the maker of the pool of water]

12.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **mourning**, you could express the same idea in other ways. Alternate translation: [for people to lament]

The terms **weeping** and **mourning** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [for deeply mourning]

Shaving one’s head and wearing sackcloth were symbolic actions by which people showed grief and repentance. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and for shaving their heads and wearing sackcloth to show their grief and repentance]

13.note: Isaiah is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [but look]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [but behold, there is joy and gladness]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **joy** and **gladness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [being joyful and glad]

The terms **joy** and **gladness** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [great rejoicing]

The people are saying the opposite of what one would expect, given that Yahweh has called them to mourn. They are feasting and celebrating instead of repenting. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Instead of mourning, let us enjoy food and drink now, for tomorrow we die]

14.note: The expression **it was revealed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh of Armies revealed in my ears]

Here, **ears** represents hearing or receiving a message. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh of Armies revealed to me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what you have done wrong]

14.q: אִם יְ֠כֻפַּר הֶ⁠עָוֺ֨ן הַ⁠זֶּ֤ה לָ⁠כֶם֙ עַד תְּמֻת֔וּ⁠ן
14.note: Following the custom of the culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [If this iniquity will be covered for you until you die, then I am not Yahweh of Armies]

The expression **will be covered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will cover this iniquity]

16.note: This is the beginning of what Yahweh told Isaiah to say to Shebna. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh. Alternate translation: [‘What to you here, and who to you here,]

16.q: מַה לְּ⁠ךָ֥ פֹה֙ וּ⁠מִ֣י לְ⁠ךָ֣ פֹ֔ה כִּֽי חָצַ֧בְתָּ לְּ⁠ךָ֛ פֹּ֖ה קָ֑בֶר
16.note: Yahweh wants Isaiah to use the question form to rebuke Shebna for presuming to prepare an elaborate tomb for himself. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You have no business being here, and you have no relatives here, yet you have hewn a tomb for yourself here]

16.q: מַה לְּ⁠ךָ֥ פֹה֙ וּ⁠מִ֣י לְ⁠ךָ֣ פֹ֔ה
16.note: Yahweh is using **What to you here, and who to you here** as a common expression of this culture to mean that the person he is addressing has no valid connection with what he describes next. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you translate this verse so that there is not a quotation within a quotation, they should do the same thing through v. 24. Alternate translation: [Tell him that he has no right to be here and has no family here]

17.note: Yahweh is telling Isaiah to tell Shebna **Behold Yahweh, hurling you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh is about to hurl you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is about to hurl you]

Isaiah is using a literary device in the original language in which a verb and its related noun are used together for emphasis. If you can express the emphasis of this figure of speech in your language, it would be appropriate to do so here. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [hurling you away violently]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **wrap** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [and he will wrap you tightly]

18.note: Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **wind** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [He will wind you as tight as a ball]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a ball** is tossed far away with great force, so Yahweh will hurl Shebna far away. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [tossing you like a ball thrown far away with great force]

The expression **a land broad of hands** was a common expression meaning “a wide, open land.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a wide, open land]

18.q: וְ⁠שָׁ֨מָּ⁠ה֙ מַרְכְּב֣וֹת כְּבוֹדֶ֔⁠ךָ קְל֖וֹן בֵּ֥ית אֲדֹנֶֽי⁠ךָ
18.note: Telling Isaiah what to tell Shebna, Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and there, the chariots of your glory will be a disgrace to the house of your lord]

Telling Isaiah what to tell Shebna, Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **chariots** that are characterized by **glory**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your glorious chariots]

Telling Isaiah what to tell Shebna, here Yahweh is speaking of the royal dynasty as if it were a **house**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your master’s family]

19.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **station** and **position**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [from your post and from your role]

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [And I will expel you from the palace; indeed, I will demote you to no work here]
Yahweh is referring to himself by using the word **one** here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and from your position, I, Yahweh, will tear you down]

20.note: Yahweh is using the phrase translated as **And it will happen** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
Isaiah is using the phrase **in that day** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at that time]

Here Yahweh is telling Isaiah to introduce Eliakim the son of Hilkiah as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [to my servant Eliakim, who is the son of Hilkiah]

21.note: Here Yahweh is telling Isaiah to tell Shebna of transferring authority to Eliakim as if it were **clothing** him with Shebna’s tunic and sash. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will give him your authority, and I will establish him in your position]

Here, **his hand** represents Eliakim’s power or control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and I will give your dominion into Eliakim’s control]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **dominion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and I will give what you rule]

Here Yahweh is speaking of Eliakim’s role as protector and leader as if he would be a **father** to the people of Jerusalem. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will be a protector and leader to the people of Jerusalem]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the people of Judah as if they were a **house**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to the people of Judah]

22.note: Here Yahweh is telling Isaiah to speak of access to the royal family as if it were a **house** to which Eliakim would hold the **key**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will put you in charge of the king and his household]

Here, **the key of the house of David** represents the authority to make decisions for the royal household. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the power to open and shut the house of David]
Here, **his shoulder** represents his responsibility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [as his responsibility]

22.q: וּ⁠פָתַח֙ וְ⁠אֵ֣ין סֹגֵ֔ר וְ⁠סָגַ֖ר וְ⁠אֵ֥ין פֹּתֵֽחַ
22.note: Yahweh is referring to all of Eliakim’s authority by naming two major components, **opening** and **shutting**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and he will have complete authority over everything]

23.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a peg** driven into a firm place is secure and unmovable, so Eliakim will be secure in his position. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a peg securely fastened in a firm place]

The expression **made firm** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [into a place that I have made firm]

Here Yahweh is speaking of Eliakim bringing honor to his family as if he were **a throne of glory**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will bring great honor to the house of his father]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **throne** that is characterized by **glory**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a glorious throne]

Here Yahweh is speaking of Eliakim’s family as if they were a **house**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the family of his father]

24.note: Here Yahweh is telling Isaiah to speak of Eliakim’s family members’ dependence on his position as if they were objects **hanging** on a peg. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they will depend on him for all the glory]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe the **glory** that belongs to **the house of his father**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the honor that belongs to the family of his father]

The terms **the offspring** and **the descendants** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [all of his descendants]

Yahweh is using the adjective **small** as a noun to mean a certain kind of vessel. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the smaller vessels]

25.note: The expression **the peg driven into a place made firm** uses a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the peg that someone drove into a firm place]

Here Yahweh is speaking of Eliakim’s secure position of authority as if it were **the peg driven into a place made firm**. He says that it **will depart**, meaning Eliakim will lose his position. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Eliakim will lose his position of authority]

The expression **it will be cut down** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and they will cut the peg down and let it fall]

The expression **the burden that was on it will be cut off** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that which was hanging on it will fall]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the people who depended on Eliakim’s position as if they were a **burden** hanging on a peg. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and all who depended on Eliakim will be cut off]

**For Yahweh has spoken** is a concluding statement that confirms the certainty of the preceding oracle. This signals the end of the prophecy. Use the natural form in your language for expressing the conclusion of a story. Alternate translation: [thus Yahweh has spoken]
